title: Long-term complication profiles following transsphenoidal and transcranial resection of adult craniopharyngioma: A retrospective cohort study
content:
by William L. Zeng, Aman Singla, David J. Cote, Sindhu Daggupati, Jonathan Dallas, Robert G. Briggs, Gabriel Zada

Introduction

Craniopharyngiomas arise in the sellar/suprasellar region and are managed with maximal safe resection via transsphenoidal (TSR) or transcranial (TCR) approaches. The optimal approach remains contested, as treatment must balance tumor control against long-term visual, endocrine, neurologic, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak–related morbidity. Longitudinal complication and morbidity profiles of craniopharyngioma resection in adults remain limited. We evaluated approach-specific long-term outcomes in a large multi-institutional adult cohort.

Methods

In a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX network, adult craniopharyngioma patients undergoing TSR or TCR were compared using unmatched analyses and propensity score matching (PSM). Matching characteristics included demographics, comorbidities, presenting features, and prior radiation. Cox models estimated hazard ratios (HR) at 1, 5, 10, and 15 years from surgery.

Results

We identified 2,558 (41.0%) patients who underwent TSR and 1,452 (23.3%) who underwent TCR. Patients selected for TCR had more preoperative hydrocephalus and diabetes insipidus (DI), whereas TSR patients had more hypopituitarism. After PSM (1,199 pairs), TSR carried higher early CSF-leak risk (1-year HR:1.65, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.25–2.19, p < 0.001) but lower rates of 1-year mortality (HR:0.54, 95%CI:0.33–0.91, p = 0.02), hydrocephalus (HR:0.35, 95%CI:0.18–0.71, p = 0.002), blindness (HR:0.54, 95%CI:0.33–0.86, p = 0.009), and adjuvant radiation (HR:0.70, 95%CI:0.52–0.94, p = 0.02). At 10 years, TSR was associated with lower hydrocephalus (HR:0.57, 95%CI:0.35–0.93, p = 0.02), DI (HR:0.69, 95%CI:0.52–0.91, p = 0.01), and blindness (HR:0.61, 95%CI:0.43–0.86, p = 0.01), but higher hypopituitarism (HR:1.24, 95%CI:1.06–1.46, p = 0.01), higher composite endocrine morbidity (HR:1.23, 95%CI:1.03–1.46, p = 0.02), and persistently elevated CSF leak (HR:1.32, 95%CI:1.02–1.72, p = 0.04). Findings at 5 and 15 years were concordant.

Conclusions

Adults with craniopharyngioma experience substantial long-term visual, endocrine, hydrocephalus-related, and treatment-related morbidity. TSR and TCR were associated with distinct long-term complication profiles, with TSR generally associated with lower rates of hydrocephalus, blindness, epilepsy, and DI but higher rates of CSF leak and hypopituitarism. These findings provide long-term population-level estimates that may inform surgical counseling and postoperative surveillance.
